subject: MCSim as a model of how to do ode in Stan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: MCSim as a model of how to do ode in Stan
parts:
What we need for Stan is to (a) come up with a language for specifying
implicit functions with ODEs and (b) solve the ODEs using an integrator
that we can differentiate. (There are known techniques for doing the auto-diff,
either by auto-diffing the integrator or integrating the auto-diff of the equations.

Frederic Bois suggested looking at his project MCSim, and it
looks really great:

http://www.gnu.org/software/mcsim/mcsim.html

Andrew worked with Frederic on modeling issues and we'll both
be working with Frederic in France next year.

The general setup is that there's an implicit multivariate function of
time x(t) that arises from a diffeq with parameters phi,

d/dt x(t) = f(x(t), t, phi),

and an initial state at time 0,

x(0) = x_0.

The desired computation is of the state after time t,

x(t) = g(x_0, t, phi).

We solve for x(t) by simulating the system from t_0

compute g by running an integrator (like the leapfrog integrator
we use for Hamiltonian systems in Stan).

The statistical problem is estimating the parameters phi from noisy
observations of x at time t. In order to run HMC, we need derivatives
w.r.t. the parameters,

d/d.phi x(t) = d/d.phi g(x_0, t, phi).

Here's an example of the kind of model in which we'd
be interested:

|
|
#---------------------------------------------------------
# Template for pharmacokinetic modeling
#---------------------------------------------------------

States = {_central, _periph};
Inputs = {_Dose_rate};
Outputs = {_Q_total};
Compartments = {central, peripheral};

# Species-dependent parameters
_PC = 2;
_K_urine;

# Species-independent parameters
V_central;
V_periph;

Initialize { _K_urine = _K_urine * 2; }

Dynamics {
_Q_rate_c_p = 5 * (_central - _periph / _PC);

# Central compartment quantity
_pk_central = (_Dose_rate - _Q_rate_c_p -
_K_urine * _central) / V_central;
dt(_central) = _pk_central;

# Peripheral compartment quantity
_pk_periph = _Q_rate_c_p / V_periph;
dt(_periph) = _pk_periph;
}

CalcOutputs { _Q_total = _central / V_central + _periph / V_periph; }

End.
|
|

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: implicitly-defined parameters
parts:
The solution for beta on (l,u) defined by

beta^5 - beta - alpha == 0
Can there be whole systems of equations?
I suppose, but I think by far the most common is just one equation.
Does anyone have an application for this?

In statistics or economics, it is usually some weird exact constraint on the parameters that has to be satisfied. These are a little easier to deal with if you are using ML because you only need the constraint to bind at the optimum and can use penalization and stuff to enforce it.

Also, some distributions do not have a closed-form PDF but may have a closed-form characteristic function or inverse CDF, such as the generalized lambda

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tukey_lambda_distribution

in which case, given a data point and the parameters, you have to solve for the implicitly-defined quantile, q,

x - icdf(q, parameters) == 0

in order to evaluate the density as a function of q (which is known in closed-form).
Any idea how we'd implement implicit functions in general?

The are usually not too difficult to solve numerically. Boost has root finders

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_54_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/internals1/roots.html

So, the question is how to is the user to communicate what arbitrary equation is to be solved. I guess we would have to parse something in the .stan file into a callable.

Or maybe this is a candidate for the model.hpp mechanism we talked about before where if model.hpp is in the same directory as model.stan the make call is

$(CC) -include model.hpp -o model $(CFLAGS) model.cpp

so we would just need to explain what model.hpp needs to #include to get it working.

Sorry if we've discussed it before --- I was very confused about
what implicit meant in the auto-diff context.

The main thing is Stan needs to know when it is dealing with an implicit function. In the above case where

x - icdf(q, parameters) == 0

you can pretty easily solve for q* on (0,1) such that this equation holds to machine tolerance, but q* is a function of the parameters. So, if you change a parameter slightly, you change q*. Thus, you have to take the derivative of

x - icdf(q, parameters)

with respect to each of the parameters and divide by the (negative of the) derivative with respect to q (at q*) in order and stick that into the autodiff expression tree in order to (correctly) evaluate the derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameters.

So, that is really a pretty different animal than an ODE, aside from the fact that in both cases you can't write what you don't know as an equation in terms of what you do know.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] implicitly-defined parameters
parts:
Thanks! That's exactly what I needed to understand
what we need to auto-diff.

Yes, very different than ode. But we might
want to use some of the same syntax for defining
equations

For syntax, since both the ode and implicit equations
define functions, some kind of function-definition syntax
seems appropriate, then you could use the function in
the code.

For the simpler case, just calling a root function might
work:

root(real beta) in { beta^5 - beta - alpha = 0; }

The icdf case seems one step more complicated in that
the function you care about is itself expressed as a derivative.
It would be nice to be able to do that, too. In fact, it's
what we need to do for the better approach to ode where we
take a Jacobian of the equation, then integrate the ode and
its Jacobian (and use the Jacobian in the solver). It's a lot of
auto-diff, but it should be doable.

- Bob

messages.author: b82af643aafe86d2
messages.subject: Re: MCSim as a model of how to do ode in Stan
parts:
In the hopes that my experience with MCSim might help with Stan's implementation of an ODE solver, I'll post a few ideas.

First: why have I used MCSim? It's probably for a somewhat different reason than most. I’ve used MCSim as a system dynamics simulator in the spirit of John Sterman’s Business Dynamics and of the System Dynamics Society (http://www.systemdynamics.org/whatisSD/). In essence, this is classical feedback control theory applied to human, organizational, and environmental systems.

From a modeling perspective, these models are characterized by systems of equations, usually expressed in integral rather than differential form for philosophical reasons, and with frequent tabular nonlinearities. Higher-end simulators make use of Kalman filtering and optimization to extract signals out of noisy data and to adjust parameters to best achieve certain goals.
Before encountering MCSim, I had created such models using iThink (isee systems), Vensim, and homebrew solutions written in Logo, Pascal, and C (built on the SimPack framework).

You can see a short example system dynamics model in MCSim in the quick reference guide at http://www.gnu.org/software/mcsim/.

What worked well in MCSim?

I’ve enjoyed working in MCSim, and I trust Frederic’s approach to crafting an expressive language for describing ODEs. Two key things impressed me about MCSim as compared to commercial simulators:

- the presence of automated solvers that eliminated the need to specify dt (you still needed to specify “stiff,” if that characterized the equations)
- that something about MCSim led me naturally to designed experiments instead of OFAT experiments on models from the very beginning

I think I was led to DOE because the models were in text, not drawn graphically, and because the model and the knowns (data and parameters) and the experiments were prespecified in separate locations.

In the hopes that these capabilities remain in the Stan ODE solver, here are a few other things I found useful.

1. the expressiveness of the language (I didn’t really miss the integral form)
2. the ability to choose one’s solver
3. thanks to deSolve, the ability to handle events (although I have yet to use them)
4. The ability to handle tabular nonlinearities with arbitrary interpolation routines using the GSL or one’s own code
5. That models were compiled and could be executed rapidly with new data without recompiling
6. that there was an xmcsim for quick prototyping, even as I only used it rarely.

I recognize that it’s unlikely for Stan to be compatible with the GSL; perhaps Boost offers similar productivity in its interpolation capabilities.  I’ve tended to use Akima interpolation because it can handle arbitrarily-spaced input resolution as well as step and linear interpolation to be compatible with commercial simulators.  I use Stineman interpolation in some cases, although I can’t think of a case where I used that in a system dynamics model.

There were things that were awkward in MCSim.

In order to facilitate tabular nonlinearities, Frederic implemented inline sections. The naming of variables became a bit arcane, as you would need different names for the same variable, depending upon whether it was in the model or the inline code.

There was no easy ability to organize equations into submodels.

As I recall (it’s been a couple of years since I’ve used MCSim regularly), MCSim’s output had two formats. I suspect most of us used R to visualize the data, it might have been handy to have standard interface routines to facilitate moving the data into a data frame (I suspect Frederic and everyone else using it developed their own.  It was easy to grab the data in gnuplot.

I generally liked MCSim’s model structure, which seems similar to that chosen for Stan. Still, most of the commercial system dynamics simulators sort the equations automatically, so you can write them in the order that makes sense to people, and the simulator reorders them so that variables are calculated in the order needed. For example, in other systems, you can order the differential equations and their supporting equations in ways that make sense to people without worrying about being sure that variables have valid values when their defining equation is executed. Perhaps something could be done with tangle inside an orgmode file that contains R and Stan code, but that still sounds manual.

Ask if something isn't clear. These are quick ideas based on my experience; there are no doubt better ways to do things. I just wanted to make sure we didn't lose the ability to do system-dynamic-type models in Stan, too.

Bill

I should've been keeping better notes, because Daniel was

The stiff solver's more constrained than some of the others
in what it does. It only works with ublas types (the matrix
lib from Boost). We might be able to get one of the non-stiff
solvers working.

This is their integrator for stiff systems:

boost_1.54.0/boost/numeric/odeint/stepper/rosenbrock4.hpp

The over-arching problem is that the assumptions about
(1) initialization and (2) variable lifespan don't play
nicely with reverse-mode auto-dif.

We were getting segfaults everywhere due to (1), though managed
to code around many of those.

The issue with lifespan is that Boost's ublas library for matrices
defines static class constants everywhere by wrapping the scalar type. And
so does the rosenbrock functions. This won't work with our variable lifespans.
We'd need traits more like those in Eigen, which seem to be modeled on the
function-based approach of std::numeric_limits. I was sort of surprised
to see Boost using static constants in ublas --- it's usually bad ju-ju in
C++ because of initialization issues. See:

/boost/numeric/ublas/matrix.hpp:
----------------------------
...
static const value_type one_;


Hmm, now that I just searched for that, I see this in vector:


boost/numeric/ublas/vector.hpp:
-------------------------------------
...
typename unit_vector<T, ALLOC>::const_value_type unit_vector<T, ALLOC>::one_ (1); // ISSUE: need 'one'-traits here


So maybe they're thinking along the same lines. They should
be calling a one_ function with traits we could specialize,
so that we could use it like +/- infinity or NaN from numeric_limits.

It nearly killed us getting it compiled as far as we did,
but I seem to recall other issues with the time type and
its interaction with the scalar type not doing the right thing.

That and one of the packages trying to use a nullary-constructed
object in some place and segfaulting. (I think we may have
coded around that, too.)

> http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_54_0/libs/numeric/odeint/doc/html/boost_numeric_odeint/tutorial/using_arbitrary_precision_floating_point_types.html

We were following this and the other clues in the doc, some of
which don't apply to Rosenbrock, because it's a special, limited
instance of their interface.
> So, I don't immediately see what additional templating is needed to utilize our types.

I can send you what we have and you can see what we've
done so far. I don't see how we can get further without further
changing their code, at which point, we'll have rewritten a lot of it.

The Rosenbrock version doesn't look too complicated to reimplement
starting from the Boost impl, and we can swap out the matrix algebra
from UBLAS with Eigen, which we already have working.

- Bob

Without looking at the docs, that sounds like the stepping in the
solution of the ODEs. That sounds like MCSim's lsodes solver: it's a
variable step size integrator. See the MCSim quick reference card at
http://www.gnu.org/software/mcsim/mcsimqrc.pdf: the first two columns of
the second page define a simple model with a simple nonlinearity to
prevent the stock called Balance from going negative. The first inline
segment defines the interpolation function, and the second executes it.

Ah, iteration. When I discovered J, I hoped I had written my last
loop. :-)

>> Ah. Will that work if I have a system of ODEs, and some RHS variables
>> are LHS results of other ODEs or LHS results of other what I'd call
>> "rate equations" -- functions of the LHS of other ODEs?

> where x is the state vector, t is time, and theta is the vector
> of model parameters. We'll have to figure out how to generalize
> this to a nice way of specifying f. Because the first examples we are
> looking at do exactly what you say.

Except for the manual ordering of equations, I like MCSim's approach
there. As with commercial system dynamics simulators, you write
something like

dt(x) = inflows - outflows;

and then perhaps

inflows = alpha * x;
outflows = - beta * x;

Make x a vector iff the RHS is common in form. For example,

dt(x) = - beta[] * x;

is nice; all the components of x decay exponentially, albeit at possibly
different rates. But write

dt(x1) = -beta * x;
dt(x2) = inflow - outflow;

because they have different form.

You might be interested in
http://www.iseesystems.com/community/support/SMILEv4.pdf and
http://www.iseesystems.com/community/support/XMILEv4.pdf, a current
attempt to create a common language for system dynamics simulators. I'm
not really encouraging you to adopt them, although feel free if they
serve your needs. The first of the two documents gives a bit of the
syntax of Dynamo, the first system dynamics language.
www.cise.ufl.edu/~fishwick/cap4800/sd2.ppt‎ gives a bit of the flavor of
that language and a few tiny models.

One reason not to adopt SMILE / XMILE is that there are other
"standards": ask Frederic about SBML.

As a total aside but related to your interest in language design, here's
the beginnings of the C-language interpreter for J:
http://www.jsoftware.com/jwiki/Essays/Incunabulum (the entire source is
at http://www.jsoftware.com/jwiki/Source).

> Definitely more than what we want to think about now, but

> units package, though I've never done more than browse it.

Interestingly, I'm not a huge fan of typing. When I don't need R's
libraries, I tend to use J for scripting, and it's a fully untyped
language.

me. I figure that 50% of the time (to a resolution of 50 percentage
points) that I have a units failure in Vensim, it's due to a typo in the
units, but in the other 50%, I have a model formulation error. I can
see that being useful in Stan generally, too.
